summary: Mars Pathfinder is a web-based EVA planning system for astronauts exploring Jezero crater on Mars. It links two interfaces: Mission Control on Earth and an Astronaut HUD that simulates the visor view. Mission Control ranks science targets with a Science Opportunity Index (SOI) built from NASA rover findings and HiRISE terrain data, then compares three walking routes by distance, slope, ascent and simulated oxygen use. A Mission Twin rehearses the traverse before the plan is approved and sent to the visor. On the HUD, the astronaut follows the approved route with suit oxygen, terrain under foot, environmental conditions, radio line of sight and a sampling checklist; field observations are saved offline and queued to sync when the link returns. Our main target is Cheyava Falls, where Perseverance found a potential biosignature. Mars Pathfinder matters because crews on foot cannot wait for Earth to answer: it turns NASA data into safe, science-driven decisions on the surface.
details:
What it does
Mars Pathfinder is a web-based EVA planning system for crews exploring Jezero crater on foot. It has two linked interfaces:

  • Mission Control (Earth).
    • Ranks science targets with a Science Opportunity Index, SOI = αM + βG + γT + δQ, scoring mineralogy, geologic context, astrobiology relevance and data quality. The weights can be adjusted.
    • Each target card states what the rover found, its limitations and how its position was obtained. For example, Cheyava Falls is described as a potential biosignature, as NASA states.
    • A traverse planner computes three routes on a 1 m HiRISE DTM (resampled to a 5 m grid): A (shortest), B (safest) and C (max science, via Bunsen Peak). It compares distance, slope, ascent, walk time and simulated O₂ budget, and plots an elevation and oxygen profile with a “bingo” line: O₂ needed to return plus 20 %.
    • An optimality check compares A* and Dijkstra on the same cost surface.
    • A Mission Twin replays the EVA at 1–30× speed, showing simulated oxygen and radio shadow before the route is approved and sent to the astronaut.
    • The astronaut follows the approved route with a compass and the distance to the target.
    • It shows suit O₂ (consumption, bingo margin, metabolic rate, EVA time), terrain under foot (slope, slip risk), environment (dust opacity, pressure, gusts, space weather, dose), the nearest shelter and radio line of sight.
    • It includes a sampling checklist and reference photos.
    • A scientific field log saves observations offline and queues them to sync when the link returns.
    • Emergency scenarios (solar event, dust gust, low O₂) can be simulated.

Benefits and impact
Crews on Mars cannot wait for Earth to answer every decision. Mars Pathfinder moves planning to Earth and gives the astronaut what they need on the surface: route, life support and science goals. The result is a safer EVA that delivers more science. The same workflow can support mission analog training on Earth, education, and site selection for future human landing studies. The challenge’s own example site, Gale crater’s boxwork at Mount Sharp, is included with Curiosity’s 2025 path and raw images.

Tools and technology
Next.js and React, rendered in WebGL and deployed on Vercel. NASA data: the HiRISE DTM and orthoimage of Jezero, Perseverance (M20) waypoints, PIXL/SHERLOC findings from the published literature (Hurowitz et al., Nature, 2025), and Curiosity raw images and traverse data for Gale. AI tools: Claude, Higgsfield and ElevenLabs were used to produce the demo video.

Creativity
It closes the loop between Earth and the visor: the same route, data and simulation flow from the planning table to the astronaut’s eyes. Science value and safety are scored together, not traded off blindly. The system also shows the limits of its data openly.

What we considered
Scientific honesty: every target shows its limitations, and a potential biosignature is not presented as a confirmed one. Crew safety: oxygen reserves with a 20 % margin, slope limits, shelter distance and radio coverage. Communication delay and blackouts, handled with offline logging. Real terrain resolution: the HUD notes that near-ground detail is limited. Usability under workload: a minimal visor layout and a guided demo.
